title: Constant-factor Π₂ hardness of approximating linear discrepancy
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
formal: Historical conjecture, resolved affirmatively: is there an absolute constant γ>1 such that distinguishing lindisc(A)≤t from lindisc(A)>γt is Π₂^P-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions, given a rational m×n matrix A and a positive rational threshold t? Here lindisc(A)=max_{w∈[0,1]ⁿ} min_{x∈{0,1}ⁿ} ‖A(w−x)‖∞. Manurangsi’s published theorem establishes the requested hardness for every fixed γ=9/8−ε with 0<ε<1/8. The source’s damaged fraction 32 referred to a 3/2 covering-radius comparison; its conjecture asks for analogous constant-factor hardness of linear discrepancy, not explicitly the identical 3/2 factor.
context:
Linear discrepancy measures the largest, over fractional vectors, of the smallest achievable row-wise rounding error. Finding a useful rounding for one given vector and estimating this worst-case value are different computational tasks.

Li and Nikolov proved NP-hardness of exact evaluation and membership of the rational threshold problem in Π₂. They conjectured analogous constant-factor Π₂ approximation hardness to the lattice covering-radius problem. Manurangsi’s 2021 theorem explicitly answers that question.

The source compares with a 3/2 covering-radius hardness result. The direct linear-discrepancy follow-up supplies a 9/8−ε factor. Its reduction has thresholds 4/3 and 3/2, whose ratio is 9/8; the occurrence of 3/2 as an absolute no-case threshold must not be mistaken for that approximation ratio.

Bennett and Ly cite Manurangsi’s published Π₂ hardness for ℓ∞ linear discrepancy and extend it to a binary covering-radius promise problem. Their work also studies finite ℓp norms. This is later progress beyond a question already settled in 2021.
why: Establishes that approximating the worst-case error of binary rounding captures the second universal level of the polynomial hierarchy, beyond ordinary NP-hardness.
status_note: Matched the original conjecture to Manurangsi’s Theorem 1 and the complete Lemma 5 reduction statement. Verified the journal publication metadata and read the September 2026 follow-up’s model and theorem. Resolution concerns some constant-factor Π₂ hardness, as explicitly claimed by the direct follow-up; no independent proof audit or proof-assistant certificate is claimed.

sentences: Linear discrepancy is the worst fractional vector’s smallest possible binary rounding error, measured in the maximum row norm.
The source conjectured that approximating this matrix quantity within some constant factor is Π₂-hard.
Manurangsi proved hardness at every factor strictly between 1 and 9/8.
The result was published in 2021 and is explicitly extended by a 2026 binary covering-radius paper.
The conjecture is resolved; the 3/2 factor mentioned in the original passage belongs to a covering-radius comparison and is not the achieved linear-discrepancy ratio.

definitions: The matrix entries and t are encoded as binary rational numerators and positive denominators; both dimensions are part of the input and unbounded. For y∈Rᵐ, ‖y‖∞=max_{j∈[m]}|y_j|. A fractional vector w ranges over the entire real cube [0,1]ⁿ and x is a binary rounding of all its coordinates. Thus the maximization is outside the minimization: a different x may be chosen for each w. The maximum exists because the minimum of finitely many continuous functions of w is continuous on a compact set. This is not discrepancy at just w=(1/2,…,1/2), and the rounding vector does not range over all integer vectors as in lattice covering radius. The promise problem accepts instances with lindisc(A)≤t and rejects those with lindisc(A)>γt; behavior in the intervening gap is unrestricted. Π₂^P consists of languages decidable by a polynomial-time predicate with one polynomial-length universal binary quantifier followed by one polynomial-length existential binary quantifier. Hardness means that every language in this class has a deterministic polynomial-time map taking its yes instances into the low-discrepancy case and its no instances into the high-discrepancy case. The factor γ is fixed before the reduction and does not depend on the matrix dimensions. A γ-approximation to the value in the one-sided convention returns v with lindisc(A)≤v≤γ lindisc(A); the gap statement avoids ambiguity about approximation conventions.
answer_criterion: The published Π₂ reduction resolves the constant-factor hardness conjecture: it has lindisc(A)≤4/3 in the yes case and lindisc(A)≥3/2 in the no case, giving hardness at every factor strictly below 9/8. This is an unconditional hardness theorem, not an unconditional proof that no polynomial-time algorithm exists. It does not establish hardness at factor 3/2, and no such stronger target is substituted for the source’s general conjecture.
